governing.name: Rinn Valley Ranch Homeowners Association, Inc.

title: Rinn Valley Ranch Turf & Putting Greens, Frederick | NoCo Turf Co.
description: Rinn Valley Ranch's guidelines never mention artificial turf, but its committee must approve a plan before any backyard landscaping. Rules, timing, lots.
h1: Rinn Valley Ranch's guidelines never mention artificial turf, but no backyard landscaping starts until the committee approves the plan.
lede: Rinn Valley Ranch is 148 lots of roughly half an acre on the west side of I-25, and its HOA's Design Review Committee looks at back yards as closely as front ones. Its documents say nothing about synthetic grass or greens. They say a great deal about plans, grades, walls, fences and ditches, and that is where a backyard design here gets decided.

answer.question: Can I put artificial turf or a putting green in a Rinn Valley Ranch backyard?
answer.answer: It depends on two sign-offs. NoCo Turf Co. installs artificial turf and putting greens in Rinn Valley Ranch, Frederick, Colorado. The HOA's Design Guidelines don't name artificial turf, but its Design Review Committee must approve a complete landscaping plan before back-yard work begins, and its page says work should also wait for the Town of Frederick's approvals and permits.

blocks.h2: The guidelines never name artificial turf or putting greens; they require an approved plan for any back-yard change.
blocks.takeaway: Silence here is neither a ban nor a pass. A green or a synthetic lawn goes to the committee as landscaping, the same way a new patio or sprinkler system would.
paras: Neither the Design Guidelines (Revision 7.2, updated December 10, 2024) nor the Declaration mentions artificial turf, synthetic grass or putting greens. What the guidelines do say is blunt. Section 3.19.1 reads: "The Design Committee requires complete landscaping plans for any changes for landscaping to front or back yards. No landscaping shall commence until plans are approved by the Design Committee."

The Declaration's list of Improvements takes in grading and changes to the drainage pattern, sprinkler systems, patios, tennis courts, sod, gravel and bark, and Section 6.4 says none may be built or altered without the committee's written approval. The exemptions in Section 4.1.3 are small ones, such as planting to an approved plan or adding plants that stay under 24 inches; every other landscaping or site change goes in for review. Colorado's rule on backyard turf follows this section, and the [HOA approval guide](/guides/hoa-turf-approval/) walks through putting a request together.

blocks.h2: Out front, 70% of the yard must be living plants, and the street-side ditch has a three-item list of its own.
paras: Section 3.19.6 requires live vegetative cover on 70% of the front yard, measured without the house, the driveway and the drainage ditch, and gravel or mulch counts only once plants, shrubs and trees are set into it. Synthetic grass isn't live cover on any plain reading, so a patch of it in front would come out of the remaining 30% along with bare rock, which has to stay in brown, gray or Colorado sandstone tones. It depends on how the committee measures your frontage; ask the DRC before a design puts turf in front of the house.

The ditch along the street is its own case. Section 3.19.4 makes each owner keep it clear so water can flow and allows only native vegetation, turf or 4- to 6-inch cobble in it. The guidelines don't say whether that "turf" means sod alone, so settle it with the committee before anything synthetic goes in the ditch.

blocks.h2: A landscaping-only request needs plans and the fee, and the committee has 30 days to answer it.
blocks.takeaway: Recent answers have come far faster than the written limit, but the Town's sign-off is a separate step.
paras: Section 4.1.1 says the committee responds within 30 days and that when only landscaping is involved, only plans and the fee are required. The guidelines don't print the fee, so ask the DRC. Requests go in through the HOA's PayHOA portal. Under Section 4.1.2 a complete request with no disapproval inside 30 days is deemed approved, and Declaration Section 6.8 says a request for more information inside that window keeps it from being deemed approved. At the August 19, 2025 board meeting the committee reported a typical 3-business-day turnaround on requests, landscaping among them.

The DRC's own page says no construction should begin until the Town of Frederick's approvals and permits are also in hand, and a plan that changes after approval must be resubmitted. Frederick's 2026 code, in force since June 1, allows artificial turf only in areas its functional-turf definition covers, a list that includes the putting green of a golf course. Whether a green behind an existing home here counts is a reading the Town makes, so put the question to Frederick's Planning Department while the committee reviews the plan.

Section 4.3 wants the work finished within 8 months of starting, with written notice of completion so the committee can inspect it. The August 2025 minutes call projects built without approval covenant violations, and the HOA's fine schedule charges $25 a month for one, starting 30 days after the first notice.

blocks.h2: A green's contours have to leave the lot draining the way the developer set it up.
paras: The guidelines want landscaping placed so the existing topography is disturbed as little as possible, with ground falling away from the house at least 1 foot in 10. Every lot has to take the runoff from lots uphill and send it to the street gutter or the back of the lot, and Declaration Section 11.3 bars interfering with the developer's drainage pattern unless the committee approves it in writing. The mounds and tiers that give a green its break are grading, which the Declaration counts as an Improvement, so draw them on the plan along with the path the water takes around them.

A tiered green that needs a retaining wall meets Section 3.12: 4 feet at most, in brick, stone, stucco or treated wood, and a wall within 2 feet of a shared lot line needs the neighbor's approval. The Declaration also warns that parts of the community may sit on potentially expansive soils, which is why every home here needs a soils report and an engineered foundation. A turf base on that ground deserves the same caution; the [clay soil guide](/guides/artificial-turf-on-clay-soil/) explains what changes underneath.

blocks.h2: On lots of about half an acre, the guidelines favor a green that flows into the neighbors' yards over one fenced off from them.
paras: The statewide parcel file counts 148 residential parcels across Rinn Valley Ranch's two filings, 70 lots in the first and 78 annexed in 2003. The median parcel is about 0.55 acre, the middle half fall between 0.50 and 0.66 acre, and the largest reach about 1.1 acres, so a green can sit well clear of the house and its drainage paths.

The guidelines spell out the look they want. Section 3.19.1 discourages any plan that draws a rigid property boundary and encourages yards that blend into one another through similar plants and random clumps of trees along lot lines, and Section 3.20, which sets no mandatory architectural style, encourages exterior courtyards and semi-enclosed patios. Patios of brick, stone or concrete may go anywhere at or below grade once the landscape requirements are met. For a green, that points toward edges finished in planting and stone, opening off a courtyard, rather than a hard outline at the property line.

Evening play needs its own approval: beyond approved porch lights, exterior lighting requires the committee's written approval, and it may allow subdued light whose source can't be seen from nearby homes.

blocks.h2: Irrigation ditches run through Rinn Valley Ranch, but their water belongs to neither the HOA nor any lot.
paras: The HOA has to maintain and repair the ditches on its plat, the Rink Lateral, the Rural Ditch and the Godding Ditch Lateral among them. Yet Declaration Section 14.11 says water in or flowing through any ditch lateral here is not owned by the Association, and the Declaration gives no owner any right to it. The Declaration hands no lot a ditch supply for its lawn.

Going by the map, tap water here comes from Left Hand Water District: the neighborhood lies west of I-25, and the Town says its residents west of I-25 are Left Hand customers, so the Town's own shortage stages don't reach these lots; Left Hand has declared its own Stage 1 (Mild) shortage and asks for voluntary cuts. The guidelines also point owners to Colorado WaterWise's xeriscape guidance.

One ditch rule matters on install day. The HOA's minutes have reminded owners that motorized vehicles may not travel along the ditch behind the homes on Cottonwood Circle and Homestead, so plan equipment access through your own lot.

faq.q: Can I put a chipping net or a fence around a green in Rinn Valley Ranch?
faq.a: Any fence change needs committee review. Section 3.13 allows an open three-rail white PVC fence set at 52 inches anywhere except the front yard and street-side yards, caps solid PVC at 6 feet and 60 linear feet per lot, and bans wire and chain link. Nets aren't named, so it depends on how the DRC reads one; ask before you order it.

faq.q: Can a pergola or shade structure go beside the green?
faq.a: With review. Section 3.17 sends every accessory structure to the committee, requires one of 200 square feet or more to match the house's finish, colors and windows, and rules out metal sheds. The setback sheet on the HOA's DRC page, for the neighborhood's R-1 zoning, keeps a detached accessory structure 55 feet from the front lot line, 15 from the side and 5 from the rear.

faq.q: What should a Rinn Valley Ranch submittal for a green show?
faq.a: Declaration Section 6.4 lets the committee ask for surveys, plot plans, drainage plans, elevations, specifications and samples of materials and colors. So place the green against the house and lot lines, give the grades before and after with the path runoff takes, and name the turf, edging, and any wall, lights or fence.

faq.q: What rules apply to the crew on install day?
faq.a: The guidelines' construction rules do. Contractor and supplier vehicles park on one side of the street only and may not drive through the ditches or onto neighboring lots, excess excavation is hauled off or placed where the committee says, debris leaves the site at least weekly, and contractors may not bring dogs into the community.

faq.q: We just moved in. When is our landscaping due?
faq.a: The DRC's page asks for complete landscaping plans within 3 months of occupancy, with every plant named and drawn at 5 years' growth, then half the landscaping finished within 12 months and the rest within 24. A green can be part of that first plan rather than a second submittal later.
